Content description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
Elaboration: responding to a request to collect a quantity of objects or reading a numeral and selecting the associated quantity of items from a collection to match the number required; for example, collecting 9 paint brushes after hearing the word ‘nine’

Content description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
Elaboration: recognising the order in the sequence of numbers to 20 and identifying the number that is “one less” than a given number and the number that is “one more”; for example, playing instructive card games that involve reading and ordering number cards; using counting songs, story books and rhymes to establish the forwards and backwards counting sequence of numbers in the context of active counting activities

Content description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
Elaboration: understanding and using terms such as “first”, “second”, “third”, … “fifth”… to indicate ordinal position in a sequence; for example, creating a number track using cards with the numerals zero to 20 and describing positions using terms such as first, last, before, after, between

Content description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
Elaboration: recognising, writing and reading numerals written on familiar objects; for example, in images, text or illustrations in story books; writing a numeral on a container as a label to show how many objects it contains

Content description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
Elaboration: connecting quantities to number names and numerals when reading and reciting stories and playing counting games or determining and reasoning about the size of sets of objects within First Nation Australians’ instructive games; for example, Segur etug from Mer Island in the Torres Strait region

Content description: recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising
Elaboration: recognising how many objects are in a collection or in images on a card with a quick look and saying the associated number without counting

Content description: recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising
Elaboration: playing instructive card games that rely on the recognition of numbers represented in different ways; for example, playing memory games, matching pairs of quantities on dot cards or similar where the arrangement on each is different; using subitising to compare and order collections and to say who has more when sharing items in a game

Content description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
Elaboration: establishing the language and process of counting, understanding that each object must be counted only once, that the arrangement of objects does not affect how many there are, and that the last number counted answers the question of “How many?”; for example, saying numbers in sequence while playing and performing actions

Content description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
Elaboration: using counting to compare the size of two or more collections of like items to justify which collection contains more or less items

Content description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
Elaboration: using counting and one-to-one correspondence to quantify the number of items required for a purpose; for example, when asked to collect enough scissors for each member of their group to have a pair, counting each member and using the total count to know how many to collect

Content description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
Elaboration: discussing how different cultures may have alternative ways of representing the count; for example, discussing how people of the Asia region use an abacus or Chinese hand gestures

Content description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
Elaboration: using body-tallying that involves body parts and one-to-one correspondence from counting systems of First Nations Peoples of Australia, to count to 20

Content description: partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships and subitising to recognise and name the parts
Elaboration: recognising numbers represented in physical or virtual ten-frames, and describing their reasoning: “It’s 7 because there is 5 there and 2 more”

Content description: partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships and subitising to recognise and name the parts
Elaboration: partitioning collections of up to 10 objects in different ways and saying the part-part-whole relationship; for example, partitioning a collection of 6 counters into 4 counters and 2 counters and saying, “6 is 4 and 2 more, it’s 2 and 4””, then partitioning the same collection into 5 and one or 3 and 3

Content description: partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships and subitising to recognise and name the parts
Elaboration: representing part-part-whole relationships in numbers up to 10 using physical or virtual materials; for example, identifying numbers represented by dots in standard number configurations such as dominos and dice by recognising parts that form the whole

Content description: partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships and subitising to recognise and name the parts
Elaboration: exploring number groupings in First Nations Australians’ counting systems and the different ways of representing these groupings to form and partition numbers, applying this to quantify collections of objects in the environment on Country/Place up to 10

Content description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: using role-play and materials to represent mathematical relationships in stories; for example, “Eight kangaroos were drinking at the river and 3 hopped away”; drawing a picture and using materials to represent the situation, discussing, and recording the result of the action with a numeral

Content description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: role playing or actively engaging in situations that involve quantifying or comparing collections of items or simple money transactions; for example, “Do we have enough scissors for our group so that each person has their own pair?”; role-playing using $1 coins to pay for items in a shop where items are priced in whole dollars

Content description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: representing situations expressed in First Nations Australians’ stories, such as “Tiddalick, the greedy frog”, that describe additive situations and their connections to Country/Place

Content description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: representing addition and subtraction situations found in leaf games involving sets of objects used to tell stories, such as games from the Warlpiri Peoples of Yuendumu in the Northern Territory

Content description: represent practical situations involving equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: using materials to role-play equal sharing; for example, sharing pieces of fruit or a bunch of grapes between 4 people and discussing how you would know they have been shared equally; when playing card games where each player is dealt the same number of cards, and counting the number of cards after the deal to ensure they have the same amount

Content description: represent practical situations involving equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: representing situations that involve counting several items; for example, 9 beads or 6 $1 coins, and sharing them equally between 3 people by subitising or counting each group by ones to decide how many beads or coins each person will receive

Content description: represent practical situations involving equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
Elaboration: exploring instructive games of First Nations Australians that involve sharing; for example, playing Yangamini of the Tiwi Peoples of Bathurst Island to investigate and discuss equal sharing

Content description: recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways
Elaboration: recognising, copying and describing different repeating patterns using materials, shapes, sounds and movements during activities and play; for example, making a bead necklace and describing the pattern they have created, such as, “red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red, blue, green”; copying repeating patterns of drumbeats or dance moves during music activities

Content description: recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways
Elaboration: recognising repeating patterns used at home and in daily activities to help make tasks easier or to solve problems; for example, setting the table to eat

Content description: recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways
Elaboration: recognising and describing repeating patterns that can be observed on Country/Place and in First Nation Australians artwork, cultural performances and material cultures; for example, shell and seed necklaces, dances and songs

Content description: identify and compare attributes of objects and events, including length, capacity, mass and duration, using direct comparisons and communicating reasoning
Elaboration: using language to describe the measurement attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, and connecting the words with the appropriate attribute; for example, using words like “tall”, “short”, “wide”, “long”, “high” to describe the attribute of length

Content description: identify and compare attributes of objects and events, including length, capacity, mass and duration, using direct comparisons and communicating reasoning
Elaboration: directly comparing pairs of objects to say which is longer/shorter, and explaining or demonstrating how they know; for example, standing back-to-back to determine who is taller; choosing to line up the bases of a spoon and fork to decide which is longer and explaining why

Content description: identify and compare attributes of objects and events, including length, capacity, mass and duration, using direct comparisons and communicating reasoning
Elaboration: starting 2 events at the same time to decide which takes longer; for example, putting on a pair of sandals with buckles or Velcro, describing the duration using familiar terms and reasoning, “I took a longer time because I’m still learning to do up my buckles”

Content description: identify and compare attributes of objects and events, including length, capacity, mass and duration, using direct comparisons and communicating reasoning
Elaboration: directly comparing pairs of everyday objects from the kitchen pantry to say which is heavier/lighter; for example, hefting a tin of baked beans and a packet of marshmallows; comparing the same pair of objects to say which is longer/shorter and discussing comparisons

Content description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
Elaboration: ordering images of daily events on a string line across the room, and justifying the placement by referring to morning, lunchtime, afternoon, and night time

Content description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
Elaboration: distinguishing between the days of the school week and weekends, and recognising that the days of the week form a sequence that repeats, with Monday always following on from Sunday

Content description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
Elaboration: sequencing the events from a story in the order in which they occurred using language like, “This happened first” then “This happened next”

Content description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
Elaboration: creating, interpreting and discussing classroom rosters; for example, a roster for watering the classroom garden and asking, “Who watered the garden yesterday?” or “Whose turn is it today?”

Content description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
Elaboration: creating a pictorial diary to show the important events that happen on the various days of the week

Content description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
Elaboration: sorting a collection of shapes into groups based on different features such as the number of sides, colour or size, and describing how they have been sorted

Content description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
Elaboration: creating a picture using a variety of shapes and a range of materials, including objects to trace around, describing the shapes they have created or used and sharing why they chose each shape in their picture

Content description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
Elaboration: creating familiar shapes using groups of people; for example, holding hands and creating a circle

Content description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
Elaboration: recognising and naming shapes that are (close to) rectangles, squares, triangles and circles in component parts of everyday items; for example, on bicycles, toy vehicles or kitchen pantry items

Content description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
Elaboration: describing and naming shapes within objects that can be observed on Country/Place, recreating and sorting into groups based on their shape

Content description: describe the position and location of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects within a familiar space
Elaboration: describing the position of an item in relation to other items in the space using language like “inside”, “underneath” and “on top of”; for example, when asked “Where are the scissors kept?”, responding with “They are in a box, on the bottom shelf at the back of the classroom”

Content description: describe the position and location of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects within a familiar space
Elaboration: describing where they have moved themselves and items in relation to other items within a space, using familiar terms; for example, playing a hiding game and when asked “Where did you hide the ball?”, responding, “I hid it behind the garbage bin over there near the bench”

Content description: describe the position and location of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects within a familiar space
Elaboration: exploring First Nations Australians’ instructive games; for example, Thapumpan from the Wik-Mungkan Peoples of Cape Bedford in north Queensland, describing position and movement of self in relation to other participants, objects or locations

Content description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
Elaboration: collecting, and sorting data collected through everyday activities or events; for example, sorting toys into categories, such as “toys that move” and “toys that don’t move”

Content description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
Elaboration: collecting and deciding how to organise data to answer “Yes/No” questions; for example, “Do more people in our class today have shoes with laces than without?”; explaining that lining up, and matching shoes with and without laces one-to-one will answer the question

Content description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
Elaboration: creating classroom charts and rosters using stickers to represent data; comparing and interpreting representations

Content description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
Elaboration: investigating statistical contexts after reading a story, such as “The Waterhole” by Graeme Base; asking and responding to questions like “What different animals did you see?”, “How many different types of animals were there?” or “Were there more tigers or kangaroos?”

Content description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
Elaboration: exploring what and how information from the environment is collected and used by First Nations Australians to predict weather events

Content description: recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals, number lines and charts
Elaboration: reading, writing and naming numerals and ordering two-digit numbers from zero to at least 120, using patterns within the natural number system, including numbers that look and sound similar; for example, 16, 60, 61 and 66

Content description: recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals, number lines and charts
Elaboration: using number tracks or positioning a set of numbered cards in the correct order and relative location by pegging on an empty number line

Content description: recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals, number lines and charts
Elaboration: using hundreds charts to build understanding and fluency with numbers; for example, collaboratively building a hundreds chart using cards numbered from zero to 99; colour code the count of tens in a hundreds chart using one colour to represent the number of tens and another to represent the number of ones

Content description: recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals, number lines and charts
Elaboration: recognising that numbers are used in all languages and cultures but may be represented differently in words and symbols; for example, through kanji numbers in Japanese and characters in Chinese, and that there are alternate numeration systems; for example, using special characters for 10 and 100 and other multiples of 10 in Japanese and Chinese numeration

Content description: partition one- and two-digit numbers in different ways using physical and virtual materials, including partitioning two-digit numbers into tens and ones
Elaboration: building knowledge and understanding of the part-part-whole facts to 10, using physical and virtual materials; for example, using virtual ten-frames through a digital app or website to identify pairs of numbers that combine to make 10

Content description: partition one- and two-digit numbers in different ways using physical and virtual materials, including partitioning two-digit numbers into tens and ones
Elaboration: using physical and virtual materials to partition numbers into counts of tens and ones; for example, recognise 35 as 3 tens and 5 ones or as 2 tens and 15 ones

Content description: partition one- and two-digit numbers in different ways using physical and virtual materials, including partitioning two-digit numbers into tens and ones
Elaboration: using part-part-whole reasoning and physical or virtual materials to represent 24, then partitioning 24 in different ways and recording the partitions using numbers; for example, 10, 10 and 4 combine to make 24 or 10 and 14 combine to make 24

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: counting a large collection of items using groups of fives or tens and skip counting to work out how many there are; recording the amount and connecting the digits in the number to the grouped materials when using groups of 10

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: counting collections of objects such as pencils or images of birds in a tree, by grouping them in tens to enable efficient counting and connecting the digits in the number to the groups of tens and ones

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: counting a large collection of Australian $1 coins by stacking them into piles of 10, skip counting in tens and including any leftover coins to determine the total value

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: using drawings, physical and virtual materials and number combinations within 10 to add and subtract collections to 20

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: adding and subtracting numbers within 20, using a variety of representations and strategies such as counting on, counting back, partitioning and part-part-whole knowledge of numbers to 10; for example, using partitioning and combining 7 + 5 = 7 + 3 + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: developing and using strategies for one-digit addition and subtraction based on part-part-whole relationships for each of the numbers to 10 and subitising with physical and virtual materials; for example, 8 and 6 is the same as 8 and 2 and 4

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: representing story problems involving addition and subtraction of numbers within 20 using a Think Board, recognising and using + and − symbols and the equal sign to represent the operations of addition and subtraction; showing and explaining the connections between any materials used using the language of plus and minus, and the numbers within the story problem

Content description: quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
Elaboration: creating and performing addition and subtraction stories told through First Nations Australians’ dances

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive situations, including simple money transactions; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling problems involving addition and subtraction presented in stories, using a Think Board to represent the problem, solving the problem using physical materials and explaining the connections between any materials used, the Think Board diagram and the numbers within the story

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive situations, including simple money transactions; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling simple money problems involving addition and subtraction using whole dollar amounts; for example, setting up a shop and role-playing practical problems of buying and selling of goods, using addition and subtraction with play money and prices in whole dollar amounts; solving the problem “I had $14 and was given $15 for my birthday” using addition to answer the problem

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive situations, including simple money transactions; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling a variety of different additive situations to solve practical problems; for example, keeping track of the number of people on a bus as it stops to pick up and drop off passengers or the number of people entering a lift

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling problems involving repeated equal group situations, such as, “How many wheels are needed for 3 cars?”, using materials and drawing a picture to show what they did, and recording the results with a number

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling practical problems involving equal sharing situations; for example, sharing a set of dominoes between the 2 players in a game, and then counting or subitising to ensure they both have the same number of tiles

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
Elaboration: modelling money problems involving equal sharing; for example, sorting coins from a money box according to their denominations, sharing the coins equally between 4 people, and using counting or subitising to ensure they have equal amounts of each denomination

Content description: recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
Elaboration: using number charts, songs, rhymes and stories to establish skip counting sequences of twos, fives and tens

Content description: recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
Elaboration: using shapes and objects to represent a growing pattern formed by skip counting; for example, using blocks or beads to represent the growing patterns 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 … and 5, 10, 15, 20 …

Content description: recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
Elaboration: recognising the patterns in sequences formed by skip counting; for example, that skip counting in fives starting from zero always results in either a 5 or zero as the final digit

Content description: recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
Elaboration: counting by twos, fives, or tens to determine how much money is in a collection of coins or notes of the same denomination; for example, 5 cent, 10 cent and $2 coins or $5 and $10 notes

Content description: recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
Elaboration: using different variations of the popular Korean counting game Sam-yuk-gu for generating skip counting pattern sequences

Content description: recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
Elaboration: interpreting a repeating pattern sequence created by someone else, noticing and describing the repeating part of the pattern and explaining how they know what comes next in the sequence

Content description: recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
Elaboration: generalising a repeating pattern by identifying the unit of repeat and representing the elements using numbers, letters or symbols; for example, representing the repeating pattern of stamp, stamp, clap, stamp clap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, clap as SSCSC SSCSC SSCSC... recognising the elements that are repeating, describing the unit of repeat as SSCSC and continuing the pattern

Content description: recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
Elaboration: recognising within the sequencing of natural numbers that 0 – 9 digits are repeated both in and between the decades and using this pattern to continue the sequence and name two-digit numbers beyond 20

Content description: recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
Elaboration: identifying the repeating patterns in First Nations Australians’ systems of counting, exploring different ways of representing numbers including oral and gestural language

Content description: recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
Elaboration: considering how the making of shell or seed necklaces by First Nations Australians includes practices such as sorting shells and beads based on colour, size and shape, and creating a repeating pattern sequence

Content description: compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
Elaboration: using a piece of string to indirectly compare the length of several objects, deciding which will fit within a space; using comparative language to describe the order: shortest, short, longer, longest

Content description: compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
Elaboration: ordering the mass of 3 or more objects such as rocks, using hefting and balance scales; using comparative language to explain the order: lightest, light, heavier, heaviest, and how they decided on the order

Content description: compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
Elaboration: pouring sand/rice/water from one container to another to compare and order the capacity of 3 or more containers; describing the order of the results in terms of which holds the most/least, and those in between

Content description: compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
Elaboration: creating sand timers from everyday items or recycled material and comparing them to order the duration of time required for the sand to run through

Content description: compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
Elaboration: investigating situations where First Nations Australians estimate, compare and communicate measurements; for example, the duration of seasons; understanding animal behaviour using the length of animal tracks; investigating capacity through water management techniques of First Nations Australians, such as traditional water carrying vessels and rock holes

Content description: measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
Elaboration: using 2 different units; for example, pop sticks and pencils, to measure the length of an object such as a desk, and explaining why the number of units used may be different

Content description: measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
Elaboration: comparing the length of 2 objects such as a desk and a bookshelf by laying multiple copies of a unit and counting to say which is longer and how much longer; explaining why they shouldn’t have gaps or overlaps between the units as this will change the length of the unit

Content description: measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
Elaboration: measuring the distance between 2 locations using footsteps, comparing the results and explaining why there may be different results; for example, referring to the different length of footsteps as using different units

Content description: measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
Elaboration: measuring and comparing the length of objects using blocks; for example, comparing the height of 2 toys by stacking blocks one on top of the other and counting how many it takes to reach the height of each object to decide which is taller

Content description: describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
Elaboration: naming, listing and using familiar units of time, such as hours, days, weeks, years,

Content description: describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
Elaboration: comparing the number of days in the months of the year and explaining how the months cycle from one year to the next

Content description: describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
Elaboration: sequencing familiar events including the representation of time with pictorial timelines

Content description: describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
Elaboration: discussing events and activities and deciding whether they would take closer to an hour, a day, a week, a month or a year; for example, it takes a day for the sun to rise and fall and rise again, but it takes less than an hour for me to walk to school

Content description: describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
Elaboration: investigating durations of time represented in First Nations Australians’ seasonal calendars

Content description: make, compare and classify familiar shapes; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment, identifying the similarities and differences between them
Elaboration: classifying a collection of shapes, including different circles, ovals, regular and irregular shapes, triangles and quadrilaterals, saying what is the same about the shapes in a group and what is different between the groups

Content description: make, compare and classify familiar shapes; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment, identifying the similarities and differences between them
Elaboration: selecting a shape from a small collection of shapes inside a bag and describing the shape by feel, so that others can name the shape and give reasons for their choice

Content description: make, compare and classify familiar shapes; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment, identifying the similarities and differences between them
Elaboration: comparing the different objects that can be built out of the same number of blocks or centi-cubes and discussing the differences between them

Content description: make, compare and classify familiar shapes; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment, identifying the similarities and differences between them
Elaboration: exploring string games used in story telling by First Nations Australians; for example, Karda from the Yandruwandha Peoples of north-east South Australia, recognising, comparing, describing and classifying the shapes made by the string and their relationship to shapes and objects on Country/Place

Content description: give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
Elaboration: interpreting and following directions around familiar locations, and understanding the meaning and importance of the words when giving directions; for example, using words like “forwards” and “backwards”, “straight ahead”, “left or right” to describe movement and giving instructions like “Keep going straight until you reach the end of this passage and then turn to your right”

Content description: give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
Elaboration: creating and following an algorithm consisting of a set of instructions to move an object to a different location; for example, role-playing being a robot and following step-by-step instructions given by another classmate to move from one place to another, only moving as instructed

Content description: give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
Elaboration: following directions to move people into different positions within a line using both ordinal and positional language to describe their position; for example, directly comparing heights and following directions using ordinal and positional language to line up in height order

Content description: give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
Elaboration: describing a familiar journey across Country/Place using directional language

Content description: acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
Elaboration: discussing methods of collecting data to answer a question, such as “What types of rubbish are found in the playground?”, sharing ideas and trying out some of the suggested methods; reviewing the data collected and explaining how they might change the way they collect data next time

Content description: acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
Elaboration: collecting and recording information on a topic of interest using lists; for example, “how many people follow a particular football team” or “what colour eyes each person has”; examining the data, to generate some questions that it could answer, then rearranging the data or collecting different data to answer the question

Content description: acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
Elaboration: creating a tally to record data while observing events such as the year level of students using the bike shed; deciding on the possible categories before the observations are taken, then reviewing the data afterwards to notice whether the tally was effective

Content description: acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
Elaboration: using star charts with stickers or emojis to represent class data; for example, using emojis on a personal feeling chart to represent how they are feeling each day or using emojis to represent activities on the class calendar

Content description: acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
Elaboration: exploring ways of representing, sharing and communicating data through stories and symbols used by First Nations Australians

Content description: represent collected data for a categorical variable using one-to-one displays and digital tools where appropriate; compare the data using frequencies and discuss the findings
Elaboration: creating a pictograph with objects or drawings; discussing the possible categories for the pictograph, arranging the objects or drawings into the categories, then reflecting on the chosen categories and deciding whether they were helpful

Content description: represent collected data for a categorical variable using one-to-one displays and digital tools where appropriate; compare the data using frequencies and discuss the findings

Content description: estimate the quantity of objects in collections and make estimates when solving problems to determine the reasonableness of calculations
Elaboration: choosing which place value they would estimate to for different situations; for example, they would estimate to the nearest 10 when estimating how many dots on a ladybird or they would estimate to the nearest 1000 when estimating crowd sizes at a venue

Content description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations including financial contexts; formulate problems using number sentences and choose calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation

Content description: follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions to investigate numbers; describe any emerging patterns

How much did Peter have to start with?” as □ – $375 = $158 and solving the problem using $375 + $158 = $533 ; solving 27 + □ = 63 using subtraction, □ = 63 – 27 or by counting on; 27, 37, 47, 57, 60, 63, so add 3 tens and 6 ones, so □ = 36

Content description: recognise and explain the connection between addition and subtraction as inverse operations, apply to partition numbers and find unknown values in number sentences

Content description: extend and apply knowledge of addition and subtraction facts to 20 to develop efficient mental strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator

Content description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts

Content description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts

Content description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts

Content description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts

Content description: identify which metric units are used to measure everyday items; use measurements of familiar items and known units to make estimates

Content description: measure and compare objects using familiar metric units of length, mass and capacity, and instruments with labelled markings

Content description: measure and compare objects using familiar metric units of length, mass and capacity, and instruments with labelled markings

Content description: measure and compare objects using familiar metric units of length, mass and capacity, and instruments with labelled markings

Content description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events

Content description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events

Content description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events

Content description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events

Content description: recognise the relationships between dollars and cents and represent money values in different ways

Content description: recognise the relationships between dollars and cents and represent money values in different ways

Content description: make, compare and classify objects, identifying key features and explaining why these features make them suited to their uses
